Kutno Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kutno, Poland

Demolished. Kutno, a private noble town founded in 1386, recorded its first Jews in 1513, with an estimated 63 residents by 1579; 18th-century institutions included a hospital and a burial society that purchased this cemetery's land. Population reached 70.2% (1,376) by 1800 and 8,978 by 1908. This cemetery, established in 1793, held the ohel of Rabbi Jehoszua Trunek (d. 1893), who led the community for over 30 years as Posek haDor and authored Yeshuot Malko. Germans devastated the site during WWII, repurposing matzevot for hardening sidewalks and courtyards; unrealized Nazi plans called for a victory monument on the grounds. Postwar, ashes from Chełmno's extermination camp were interred here alongside ghetto and execution victims; the last funeral occurred in 1948. Subsequent decades saw the site used as a gravel pit, illegal dump, and pasture, with grave-robbing for valuables reported; a Holocaust monument itself was later destroyed. In the 1980s, the former Kutno Museum director and Society of Friends of the Kutno Region members recovered several hundred matzevot, allowing near-complete reconstruction of 90 tombstones and partial reconstruction of 60 more, now stored at the Regional Museum. The cemetery entered Poland's Register of Monuments (no. 635) on December 9, 1992, with a new memorial unveiled in 1993.
